w: What's tested His drawing of the Sertoli cells, which he said is on the exam How the testis is built, and which cells are inside or outside the tubules Sertoli cells and the blood-testis barrier LH goes to Leydig cells; FSH goes to Sertoli cells The steps from stem cell to sperm, and the names for each step The ducts in order, and the two vessels in the spermatic cord What the epididymis does What each gland adds to semen How an erection happens Dr. Herr's lecture on Friday, November 6 follows sperm from where they are made to where they leave the body. These notes are from his recording and his slides. He said one drawing is on the exam, the Sertoli cell drawing below, and that he won't test stained slides, only drawings. The testis The testis has a thick outer coat, the tunica albuginea, and is split into about 250 lobules. Each lobule holds a few long, coiled tubes called seminiferous tubules. Sperm are made inside these tubes. Think of it from the outside in. Between the tubes is loose tissue with blood vessels and the Leydig cells. The wall of each tube has myoid cells. Inside the wall is the lining, which has only two kinds of cells: Sertoli cells and the cells turning into sperm. The testes drop into the scrotum before birth because making sperm needs it a little cooler: about 35 degrees Celsius, not 37, on his slides. Dr. Madison's physiology lecture says about 34; both mean a few degrees cooler. About 200 million sperm are made each day. Two hormones, two cells Remember two chains. LH, Leydig, testosterone. LH tells the Leydig cells to make testosterone, which drives sperm making. FSH, Sertoli, binding protein. FSH tells the Sertoli cells to make androgen-binding protein, which keeps testosterone high inside the tubes. Each has a brake. Testosterone turns LH down. Inhibin from Sertoli cells turns FSH down. So if a man injects testosterone, his LH drops and his Leydig cells slow down. Sertoli cells He calls Sertoli cells "the refrigerator": they feed the growing sperm. Each one is tall. It stands on the base of the tube and reaches all the way to the middle. The nucleus is oval. Neighboring Sertoli cells are sealed together near their bases by tight junctions. That seal is the blood-testis barrier. It splits the tube into a bottom part, the basal compartment, where the stem cells sit, and an inner part, the adluminal compartment, where the cells in meiosis and the young sperm are hidden from the immune system. He said you need to know the difference. The drawing on the exam, from the outside in: the basal lamina, a type A and a type B stem cell, the seal between two Sertoli cells, then a primary spermatocyte, an early spermatid and a late spermatid at the middle of the tube. Sertoli cells feed and hold the growing sperm, eat the extra cytoplasm the sperm throw away, and make three things: androgen-binding protein, inhibin, and anti-Müllerian hormone, which stops the female tract from forming in a male embryo. They stop dividing in adults, and they are tough: heat, radiation and toxins don't kill them easily. Sertoli cells are inside the tubes. Leydig cells are outside. Leydig cells make testosterone before birth, at puberty and all through adult life. From stem cell to sperm The names look alike, so slow down. Spermatogenesis is the whole thing. It starts with stem cells called spermatogonia, at the bottom of the tube. They start dividing at puberty, pushed by testosterone. Dark type A cells are the reserve. Their nucleus has a little hole, a vacuole, and the nucleolus sits at the edge. Pale type A cells are lighter, with no vacuole and the nucleolus in the middle. They make type B cells. Type B cells become primary spermatocytes, which move right away past the barrier. The primary spermatocyte does meiosis, two divisions. It starts with a full set of chromosomes and ends as spermatids with half a set. Then spermiogenesis reshapes each spermatid into a sperm: the nucleus shrinks into the head, the Golgi makes the acrosome cap, the mitochondria go to the middle piece to power the tail, a tail grows, and most of the cytoplasm is thrown away. Spermiation is the sperm letting go of the Sertoli cell. He said the whole process takes about 74 days; Dr. Madison's physiology lecture says about two months. On a slide, neighboring tubes look different because each spot in a tube is at a different stage. That's normal. The ducts Sperm leave in this order: seminiferous tubule, straight tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra. Don't mix up efferent (before the epididymis) and deferens (after it). Rete testis: a network of channels with short, cube-shaped cells. Efferent ductules: 10 to 12 small ducts. Short cells and tall cells with real, moving cilia take turns, so the edge looks bumpy. The short cells soak up fluid; the cilia push sperm along. Epididymis: one long coiled duct on top of the testis, 4 to 6 meters, so a slide shows it cut many times. Tall cells with stereocilia, which are long microvilli that don't move and soak up fluid, over small basal cells that make new tall cells. Full of sperm. Vas deferens: the same lining, but a straight tube with a thick muscle wall. Easy rule: real cilia, efferent ductules; stereocilia, epididymis and vas. The vas runs in the spermatic cord. He said the only other two parts of the cord to know are the testicular artery, which brings blood to the testis, and the pampiniform plexus, a net of veins named for a vine's curling tendrils. The vas and the seminal vesicle's duct join to make the ejaculatory duct, which runs through the prostate. The epididymis It has three jobs: it finishes the sperm over 2 to 12 days, it stores them, and it moves them along by squeezing. While sperm finish there, they gain forward swimming, new surface proteins and steadier DNA. The epididymis also makes glycerophosphocholine, which stops capacitation. Capacitation, the last step before a sperm can fertilize, happens later, in the female tract. The glands Seminal vesicles: about 70 percent of semen (Dr. Madison says 50 to 80 percent). Fructose for energy, plus prostaglandins. Their cells hold a yellow pigment that glows under ultraviolet light, which helps crime labs find semen stains. Prostate: it wraps around the urethra, so a big prostate can make it slow or hard to urinate. Its fluid is the first part of the ejaculate: citric acid, acid phosphatase, an enzyme that thins the semen, and PSA, a tumor marker. It lowers the acid that urine leaves in the urethra, which would kill sperm. Older men often have hard, calcified little bodies in the gland; nobody knows what they mean. Bulbourethral, or Cowper's, glands: slippery mucus before semen comes out, to lubricate. It empties into the urethra in the penis. On a slide, look for skeletal muscle between the glands; skeletal muscle means voluntary control. An average ejaculate is about 3 milliliters, and about a quarter of the sperm in it are abnormal or don't swim. A vasectomy cuts the vas deferens. The glands that make most of the fluid join the tract after that point, so the amount of semen hardly changes; only the sperm are missing. Erection Three steps: relax, fill, trap. The smooth muscle in the arteries and the spongy tissue relaxes, so blood rushes into the two corpora cavernosa. The spaces fill and swell. The swelling presses the veins against the tough outer coat, the tunica albuginea, so the blood is trapped. The trap question is that the muscle relaxes; it does not tighten. The urethra runs through the corpus spongiosum, which fills much less, so the urethra stays open. His teacher's memory trick: "point and shoot." Erection is parasympathetic; ejaculation is sympathetic.
